extracted.intended_audience: press officers, communications staff, and science journalists evaluating or preparing science press releases
extracted.subtask_description: A checklist-style rubric to evaluate whether a science-focused press release meets international journalism ethics and intake expectations (as framed from WFSJ Guiding Principles). Useful for press officers to pre-check releases and for journalists screening pitches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release supply facts the journalist can verify against the source paper / dataset / study within minutes?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete, verifiable facts (exact sample sizes, effect sizes, p-values/confidence intervals, DOI or data links). Avoid vague claims. Include links to the source study, raw data or protocol where possible so journalists can quickly corroborate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Are sources clearly identified with their institutional role and qualifications, so the journalist can assess expertise and bias?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify named authors, their institutional affiliations and roles (PI, corresponding author), and relevant expertise or limitations. Avoid anonymous, unclear, or promotional titles that obscure actual qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-of-interest disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release reveal funding, financial ties, and competing interests at the top of the release rather than burying them?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State funding sources, sponsor roles, industry partnerships, and any potential competing interests prominently (not hidden in fine print). Include whether funders had any part in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, or the decision to publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press-release scrutiny passed pre-emptively
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release acknowledge its own promotional posture and avoid sensationalizing? Releases that anticipate the journalist's scrutiny ('this is a preliminary finding requiring replication') earn trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly flag limitations and preliminary status; avoid hype language. Use measured framing and, where appropriate, caveats about sample size, replication needs, generalizability, and alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent expert availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release supply contact info for at least one unaffiliated expert who can comment to the journalist?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide contact details (name, affiliation, email/phone) for at least one independent, unaffiliated expert able to comment on the work. This helps journalists obtain impartial perspectives and is often required by reputable outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release communicate confidence intervals, the preliminary nature of findings, and remaining unknowns?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report statistical uncertainty (CIs, margins of error), limits of inference, and what is not known. Avoid presenting tentative results as definitive; explicitly state degree of confidence and the conditions under which conclusions hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargo discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release respect the journal embargo and clearly state lift time/date so the journalist can plan coverage?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly label embargo status and exact embargo lift date/time. Do not release information early that would breach embargo; follow journal/publisher embargo rules and state any media conditions or restrictions transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced context
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release include relevant counter-perspectives or alternative interpretations rather than presenting a single-study conclusion?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate findings within the broader literature, note conflicting evidence or uncertainties, and quote or reference alternative interpretations where relevant. Avoid implying single-study results resolve larger debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-quality differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release explicitly identify the level of evidence (peer-reviewed, preprint, conference abstract, anecdotal) and avoid conflating types?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether the work is peer-reviewed, a preprint, a conference abstract, or anecdotal. Make clear differences in evidentiary weight and do not present lower-quality evidence as equivalent to peer-reviewed studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release resist overstating significance, novelty, or certainty? WFSJ explicitly flags 'first ever,' 'breakthrough,' 'miracle,' 'cure' claims for scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hyperbolic terms ('breakthrough', 'miracle', 'cure', 'first ever') unless incontrovertibly justified. Prefer measured language about contribution and limits; if novel claims are made, provide strong supporting evidence and contextualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: False-balance avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When scientific consensus is well-established (vaccines, climate, evolution), the release should not give equal time to fringe positions just to appear balanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not manufacture balance by elevating minority or debunked views to the same platform as consensus science. Provide proportionate representation: quote minority views only when they have substantive, credible evidence or when context requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote sources from multiple institutions, geographic regions, and demographic backgrounds where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a range of expert voices to avoid institutional echo chambers. Diversity of geographical and institutional perspectives improves credibility and helps journalists find varied commentators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: The release should not impose conditions (e.g., right to review the journalist's article pre-publication) that would compromise editorial independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include clauses or expectations that limit a journalist's ability to report independently (no pre-publication review rights, content approval, or restrictive terms). Make clear that provided materials are for reporting, not for negotiated approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-interest framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases should articulate why the finding matters to the journalist's public, not only to the issuing institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain relevance, potential impact, and who is affected. Avoid institution-centric framing that emphasizes prestige over public significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pickup-worthiness / defensibility check
rubrics_metrics.description: A release that pre-satisfies WFSJ principles passes intake at reputable science journalism outlets; violations of certain principles lead to filtering out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists use these principles as an intake defensibility check. Releases that violate sensationalism (principle 4), lack independent experts (5), conflate evidence quality (9), or exaggerate (10) are often filtered out even if the science is sound. Ensure release meets core accuracy, transparency, and independence criteria to be considered pickup-worthy.
